topics.topic: Whether final-component O_NONBLOCK plus a regular-file check suffices, or opening any non-regular file must be guaranteed not to block or activate it
questions: Is merely opening the final component with `O_NONBLOCK` and then checking that it is regular sufficient, or must opening every non-regular Linux file be guaranteed not to block even where Linux permits a device or filesystem to ignore or only partly honor `O_NONBLOCK`?

Is merely opening the final component with `O_NONBLOCK` the complete requirement, or must the kernel guarantee that opening every non-regular Linux file can never block even where that file type's documented open behavior does not provide that guarantee?

Must opening the final component be guaranteed not to block or activate a special file before its regular-file check, or is opening it with `O_NONBLOCK` and checking it afterward sufficient even though Linux does not guarantee nonblocking behavior for every non-regular file type?

quotes:
A17 rule 1 (and through "here and in rule 2" the secret files) opens
      each component with `O_NOFOLLOW`, whose presence no code tests; the
      configuration path must be absolute or the start is refused (as the
      secret files' paths already were), so the walk always starts at the
      root directory and no working directory is read; each directory on the way with `O_PATH` and `O_DIRECTORY`
      so that a search-only directory such as a home of mode 0711 is passed,
      `.` and `..` opened as named and empty components skipped, a path
      naming no component unreadable, the last component opened with
      `O_NONBLOCK` so that a FIFO is refused rather than waited on, and no
      such descriptor inherited by a process the kernel starts; any
      component that cannot be opened so makes the file unreadable (State 2
      rounds 129–132, State 5 rounds 145–147).

Left open on purpose (owner, 2026-10-18). State 2 round 134 asked
      which Linux release or documentation fixes "acts as Linux documents
      it", and what a device file that blocks even under `O_NONBLOCK` at the
      configuration path does. No version is named, by the owner's
      decision; a device there can be placed only by whoever already rules
      the host. Neither is answered here, and a later round that asks again
      is answered by this paragraph.
judgement.why: State 6 specifies the O_NONBLOCK procedure and records the owner's deliberate decision not to require defined behavior for a device that can still block.

topics.topic: Which Linux documentation, kernel version, and filesystem semantics define the supported baseline
questions: Which Linux documentation and semantic baseline decides whether a kernel or filesystem is supported when no Linux version is named and documented behavior differs by kernel version or filesystem?
